contentBlocks.text: This week you've learned exponential functions and their graphs. Today: a real-world growth application!

Compound interest is a classic real-world exponential growth model: an account with a starting balance P and an annual interest rate r grows according to A = P(1+r)ᵗ, where t is the number of years. Notice this matches yesterday's y=a·bˣ form, with a=P and b=(1+r). If $1,000 is deposited in an account earning 10% annual interest, find the account's balance after 2 years using A = P(1+r)ᵗ.
You just modeled real compound interest growth! Tomorrow we'll look at a real-world decay example.

objectives: Understand the compound interest formula A = P(1+r)ᵗ as an exponential growth model
Correctly calculate the balance after 2 years at 10% interest on $1,000
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review this week's exponential-function and graphing work.
2. Introduce the compound interest formula, connecting it explicitly to the y=a·bˣ form.
3. Have the child calculate the 2-year balance.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's exponential-decay lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: calculate one year at a time (year 1: 1000×1.1=1100, year 2: 1100×1.1=1210) rather than using the exponent directly
Ready for more: ask the child to calculate the balance after 3 years and compare how much was earned in year 3 alone versus year 1 alone
This is a genuinely practical, real-world application students will actually encounter with savings accounts and investments
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Common Core Algebra 2 standard F-LE.2: constructing exponential functions to model real-world growth, continuing this week's thread with a genuinely practical application.

generationData.instructions: Solve each compound interest problem using A = P(1+r)ᵗ.

$2,000 deposited at 5% annual interest. Find the balance after 2 years.
